solution:
Two angles are co-terminal when their difference is an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Here \(210^\circ - (-150^\circ) = 360^\circ = 1 \times 360^\circ\), which is an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Hence the two angles have the same terminal arm. Yes, \(210^\circ\) and \(-150^\circ\) are co-terminal.

Difference \(= 360^\circ - (-30^\circ) = 390^\circ\).
Since \(390^\circ = 1 \times 360^\circ + 30^\circ\), it is not an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Hence the terminal arms are different. No, \(360^\circ\) and \(-30^\circ\) are not co-terminal.

Difference \(= 540^\circ - (-180^\circ) = 720^\circ = 2 \times 360^\circ\), an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Hence the two angles have the same terminal arm. Yes, \(-180^\circ\) and \(540^\circ\) are co-terminal.

Difference \(= 675^\circ - (-405^\circ) = 1080^\circ = 3 \times 360^\circ\), an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Hence the two angles have the same terminal arm. Yes, \(-405^\circ\) and \(675^\circ\) are co-terminal.

Difference \(= 860^\circ - 580^\circ = 280^\circ\).
Since \(280^\circ\) is not an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\), the terminal arms are different.
No, \(860^\circ\) and \(580^\circ\) are not co-terminal.

Difference \(= 900^\circ - (-900^\circ) = 1800^\circ = 5 \times 360^\circ\), an integral multiple of \(360^\circ\).
Hence the two angles have the same terminal arm. Yes, \(900^\circ\) and \(-900^\circ\) are co-terminal.

The measure is negative, so the initial ray is rotated clockwise through \(140^\circ\).
Adding one complete rotation, \(-140^\circ + 360^\circ = 220^\circ\), so the terminal arm is the same as that of \(220^\circ\).
Since \(180^\circ < 220^\circ < 270^\circ\), the terminal arm lies in the third quadrant.
Hence \(-140^\circ\) lies in the third quadrant.
diagramNote: Angle in standard position: initial ray along the positive X-axis, rotated clockwise through 140 degrees; terminal arm in the third quadrant (co-terminal with 220 degrees).

solution:
The measure is positive and less than \(360^\circ\), so the initial ray is rotated anticlockwise through \(250^\circ\).
Since \(180^\circ < 250^\circ < 270^\circ\), the terminal arm lies in the third quadrant.
Hence \(250^\circ\) lies in the third quadrant.
diagramNote: Angle in standard position: initial ray along the positive X-axis, rotated anticlockwise through 250 degrees; terminal arm in the third quadrant.

solution:
\(420^\circ = 360^\circ + 60^\circ\), so after one complete anticlockwise rotation the ray turns a further \(60^\circ\).
The terminal arm is therefore the same as that of \(60^\circ\), and \(0^\circ < 60^\circ < 90^\circ\).
Hence \(420^\circ\) lies in the first quadrant.
diagramNote: One full anticlockwise rotation plus 60 degrees; terminal arm in the first quadrant (co-terminal with 60 degrees).

diagramNote: Two full anticlockwise rotations plus 30 degrees; terminal arm in the first quadrant (co-terminal with 30 degrees).

The measure is negative, so the initial ray is rotated clockwise through \(80^\circ\).
\(-80^\circ + 360^\circ = 280^\circ\), so the terminal arm is the same as that of \(280^\circ\).
Since \(270^\circ < 280^\circ < 360^\circ\), the terminal arm lies in the fourth quadrant.

solution:
To convert degrees to radians, multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
\(85^\circ = 85 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{85\pi}{180} = \frac{17\pi}{36}\).
Hence \(85^\circ = \left(\frac{17\pi}{36}\right)^{c}\).

To convert degrees to radians, multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
\(250^\circ = 250 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{250\pi}{180} = \frac{25\pi}{18}\).
Hence \(250^\circ = \left(\frac{25\pi}{18}\right)^{c}\).

To convert degrees to radians, multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
\(-132^\circ = -132 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{-132\pi}{180} = \frac{-11\pi}{15}\).
Hence \(-132^\circ = \left(\frac{-11\pi}{15}\right)^{c}\).

First express the angle in degrees only: \(30' = \left(\frac{30}{60}\right)^\circ = (0.5)^\circ\), so \(65^\circ 30' = (65.5)^\circ = \left(\frac{131}{2}\right)^\circ\).
Now multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\): \(\frac{131}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{131\pi}{360}\).
Hence \(65^\circ 30' = \left(\frac{131\pi}{360}\right)^{c}\).

First express the angle in degrees only: \(30' = \left(\frac{30}{60}\right)^\circ = (0.5)^\circ\), so \(75^\circ 30' = (75.5)^\circ = \left(\frac{151}{2}\right)^\circ\).
Now multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\): \(\frac{151}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{151\pi}{360}\).
Hence \(75^\circ 30' = \left(\frac{151\pi}{360}\right)^{c}\).

First express the angle in degrees only: \(48' = \left(\frac{48}{60}\right)^\circ = (0.8)^\circ\), so \(40^\circ 48' = (40.8)^\circ = \left(\frac{204}{5}\right)^\circ\).
Now multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\): \(\frac{204}{5} \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{204\pi}{900} = \frac{51\pi}{225} = \frac{17\pi}{75}\).
Hence \(40^\circ 48' = \left(\frac{51\pi}{225}\right)^{c} = \left(\frac{17\pi}{75}\right)^{c}\).

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
\(\frac{7\pi}{12} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 7 \times 15 = 105\).
Hence \(\left(\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)^{c} = 105^\circ\).

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
\(\frac{-5\pi}{3} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = -5 \times 60 = -300\).
Hence \(\left(\frac{-5\pi}{3}\right)^{c} = -300^\circ\).

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
\(5 \times \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{900}{\pi}\).
Hence \(5^{c} = \left(\frac{900}{\pi}\right)^{\circ}\).

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
\(\frac{11\pi}{18} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 11 \times 10 = 110\).
Hence \(\left(\frac{11\pi}{18}\right)^{c} = 110^\circ\).

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
\(\frac{-1}{4} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{-45}{\pi}\).
Taking \(\pi \approx 3.1416\), \(\frac{-45}{\pi} \approx -14.3239\), and \(0.3239 \times 60 \approx 19\), so this is about \(-14^\circ 19'\).
Hence \(\left(\frac{-1}{4}\right)^{c} = \left(\frac{-45}{\pi}\right)^{\circ} \approx -14^\circ 19'\).
_note: The printed key gives the approximation as "14 degrees 19 minutes" without the minus sign, although it correctly shows the exact value as (-45/pi) degrees. The angle is negative, so the approximation must be -14 degrees 19 minutes.

solution:
Separate the whole degrees from the decimal part: \((183.7)^\circ = 183^\circ + (0.7)^\circ\).
Since \(1^\circ = 60'\), \((0.7)^\circ = 0.7 \times 60' = 42'\).
Hence \((183.7)^\circ = 183^\circ 42'\).

First convert to degrees by multiplying by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\): \(\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{36}{\pi}\).
Taking \(\pi \approx 3.1416\), \(\frac{36}{\pi} \approx (11.4592)^\circ = 11^\circ + (0.4592)^\circ\).
\((0.4592)^\circ = 0.4592 \times 60' \approx (27.55)' = 27' + (0.55)'\), and \((0.55)' = 0.55 \times 60'' \approx 33''\).
Hence \(\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{c} = \left(\frac{36}{\pi}\right)^{\circ} \approx 11^\circ 27' 33''\).

Convert \(m\angle A\) to degrees: \(\frac{7\pi}{36} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 7 \times 5 = 35\), so \(m\angle A = 35^\circ\).
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(m\angle A + m\angle B + m\angle C = 180^\circ\).
\(\therefore m\angle C = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 120^\circ = 25^\circ\).
In radians, \(25 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{36}\).
Hence \(m\angle C = 25^\circ = \left(\frac{5\pi}{36}\right)^{c}\).

Convert the given angles to degrees: \(\frac{5\pi}{9} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 5 \times 20 = 100\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{18} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 5 \times 10 = 50\).
The angles of a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\), so the third angle \(= 180^\circ - 100^\circ - 50^\circ = 30^\circ\).
In radians, \(30 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
Hence the third angle is \(30^\circ = \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)^{c}\).

In a right angled triangle one angle is \(90^\circ\), so the two acute angles add up to \(90^\circ\).
Let the acute angles be \(4x\) and \(5x\) degrees. Then \(4x + 5x = 90\), so \(9x = 90\) and \(x = 10\).
\(\therefore\) the acute angles are \(40^\circ\) and \(50^\circ\), and the third angle is \(90^\circ\).
In radians, \(40 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{2\pi}{9}\), \(50 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{18}\), \(90 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Hence the angles are \(40^\circ, 50^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), that is \(\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right)^{c}, \left(\frac{5\pi}{18}\right)^{c}\) and \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{c}\).

First express the sum in degrees: \(5\pi^{c} = 5\pi \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 900^\circ\).
Let the angles be \(x^\circ\) and \(y^\circ\) with \(x > y\). Then \(x + y = 900\) and \(x - y = 60\).
Adding, \(2x = 960\), so \(x = 480\); subtracting, \(2y = 840\), so \(y = 420\).
Hence the angles are \(480^\circ\) and \(420^\circ\).

Let the angles be \(3x, 7x\) and \(8x\) degrees. Their sum is \(180^\circ\), so \(3x + 7x + 8x = 180\), i.e. \(18x = 180\) and \(x = 10\).
\(\therefore\) the angles are \(30^\circ, 70^\circ\) and \(80^\circ\).
In radians, \(30 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{6}\), \(70 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{7\pi}{18}\), \(80 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{4\pi}{9}\).
Hence the angles are \(30^\circ, 70^\circ\) and \(80^\circ\), that is \(\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)^{c}, \left(\frac{7\pi}{18}\right)^{c}\) and \(\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right)^{c}\).

Since the angles are in A.P., let them be \((a - d)^\circ, a^\circ, (a + d)^\circ\) with \(d > 0\).
Their sum is \(180^\circ\), so \(3a = 180\) and \(a = 60\).
The greatest angle is \(5\) times the least: \(60 + d = 5(60 - d)\), so \(60 + d = 300 - 5d\), giving \(6d = 240\) and \(d = 40\).
\(\therefore\) the angles are \(20^\circ, 60^\circ\) and \(100^\circ\).
In radians, \(20 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{9}\), \(60 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{3}\), \(100 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{9}\).
Hence the angles are \(20^\circ, 60^\circ\) and \(100^\circ\), that is \(\left(\frac{\pi}{9}\right)^{c}, \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\) and \(\left(\frac{5\pi}{9}\right)^{c}\).

Convert the second angle to degrees: \(\frac{\pi}{3} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 60\), so the two adjacent angles are \(40^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\).
In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles are supplementary.
The angle opposite the \(40^\circ\) angle \(= 180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ\), and the angle opposite the \(60^\circ\) angle \(= 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\).
Hence the angles of the quadrilateral, taken in order, are \(40^\circ, 60^\circ, 140^\circ\) and \(120^\circ\).

Convert the given angle to degrees: \(\frac{2\pi}{5} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 2 \times 36 = 72\), so that angle is \(72^\circ\).
The angles of a quadrilateral add up to \(360^\circ\), so the other three add up to \(360^\circ - 72^\circ = 288^\circ\).
Let them be \(2x, 3x\) and \(4x\) degrees. Then \(9x = 288\), so \(x = 32\), giving \(64^\circ, 96^\circ\) and \(128^\circ\).
In radians, \(64 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{16\pi}{45}\), \(96 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{8\pi}{15}\), \(128 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{32\pi}{45}\).
Hence the other three angles are \(64^\circ, 96^\circ\) and \(128^\circ\), that is \(\left(\frac{16\pi}{45}\right)^{c}, \left(\frac{8\pi}{15}\right)^{c}\) and \(\left(\frac{32\pi}{45}\right)^{c}\).

A regular pentagon has \(n = 5\) sides, and the exterior angles add up to \(360^\circ\).
Exterior angle \(= \frac{360^\circ}{5} = 72^\circ = 72 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)^{c}\).
Interior angle \(= 180^\circ - 72^\circ = 108^\circ = 108 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right)^{c}\).
Hence the exterior angle is \(72^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)^{c}\) and the interior angle is \(108^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right)^{c}\).

A regular hexagon has \(n = 6\) sides, and the exterior angles add up to \(360^\circ\).
Exterior angle \(= \frac{360^\circ}{6} = 60^\circ = 60 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).
Interior angle \(= 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ = 120 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).
Hence the exterior angle is \(60^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\) and the interior angle is \(120^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)^{c}\).

A regular heptagon has \(n = 7\) sides, and the exterior angles add up to \(360^\circ\).
Exterior angle \(= \frac{360^\circ}{7} \approx (51.43)^\circ\), and in radians \(\frac{360}{7} \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)^{c}\).
Interior angle \(= 180^\circ - \frac{360^\circ}{7} = \frac{900^\circ}{7} \approx (128.57)^\circ\), and in radians \(\frac{900}{7} \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{5\pi}{7}\right)^{c}\).
Hence the exterior angle is \((51.43)^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)^{c}\) and the interior angle is \((128.57)^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{5\pi}{7}\right)^{c}\).

A regular octagon has \(n = 8\) sides, and the exterior angles add up to \(360^\circ\).
Exterior angle \(= \frac{360^\circ}{8} = 45^\circ = 45 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{c}\).
Interior angle \(= 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ = 135 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)^{c}\).
Hence the exterior angle is \(45^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{c}\) and the interior angle is \(135^\circ\) or \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)^{c}\).

In one hour the minute-hand turns \(360^\circ\) and the hour-hand \(30^\circ\), so in one minute they turn \(6^\circ\) and \((0.5)^\circ\) respectively.
At ten past eleven, i.e. \(11{:}10\), measuring clockwise from 12 the hour-hand is at \(11 \times 30^\circ + 10 \times (0.5)^\circ = 335^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(10 \times 6^\circ = 60^\circ\).
Difference \(= 335^\circ - 60^\circ = 275^\circ\), so the angle between the hands is \(360^\circ - 275^\circ = 85^\circ\).
Hence the required angle is \(85^\circ\).

The hour-hand turns \((0.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand \(6^\circ\) per minute.
At twenty past seven, i.e. \(7{:}20\), the hour-hand is at \(7 \times 30^\circ + 20 \times (0.5)^\circ = 210^\circ + 10^\circ = 220^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(20 \times 6^\circ = 120^\circ\).
Difference \(= 220^\circ - 120^\circ = 100^\circ\), which is less than \(180^\circ\).
Hence the required angle is \(100^\circ\).

The hour-hand turns \((0.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand \(6^\circ\) per minute.
At thirty five past one, i.e. \(1{:}35\), the hour-hand is at \(1 \times 30^\circ + 35 \times (0.5)^\circ = 30^\circ + (17.5)^\circ = (47.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(35 \times 6^\circ = 210^\circ\).
Difference \(= 210^\circ - (47.5)^\circ = (162.5)^\circ\), and \((0.5)^\circ = 30'\).
Hence the required angle is \(162^\circ 30'\).

The hour-hand turns \((0.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand \(6^\circ\) per minute.
Quarter to six is \(5{:}45\); the hour-hand is at \(5 \times 30^\circ + 45 \times (0.5)^\circ = 150^\circ + (22.5)^\circ = (172.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(45 \times 6^\circ = 270^\circ\).
Difference \(= 270^\circ - (172.5)^\circ = (97.5)^\circ\), and \((0.5)^\circ = 30'\).
Hence the required angle is \(97^\circ 30'\).

The hour-hand turns \((0.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand \(6^\circ\) per minute.
At \(2{:}20\), the hour-hand is at \(2 \times 30^\circ + 20 \times (0.5)^\circ = 60^\circ + 10^\circ = 70^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(20 \times 6^\circ = 120^\circ\).
Difference \(= 120^\circ - 70^\circ = 50^\circ\), which is less than \(180^\circ\).
Hence the required angle is \(50^\circ\).

The hour-hand turns \((0.5)^\circ\) and the minute-hand \(6^\circ\) per minute.
At \(10{:}10\), the hour-hand is at \(10 \times 30^\circ + 10 \times (0.5)^\circ = 300^\circ + 5^\circ = 305^\circ\) and the minute-hand at \(10 \times 6^\circ = 60^\circ\).
Difference \(= 305^\circ - 60^\circ = 245^\circ\), so the angle between the hands is \(360^\circ - 245^\circ = 115^\circ\).
Hence the required angle is \(115^\circ\).
